chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qashani, from Abu Ayyub Suleiman ibn Muqatil al-Madani, from Dawud ibn Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Ja'fari, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was in

one of his military expeditions, so a group of riders passed by him while he was praying. They stopped by the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and asked them about the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), supplicated, praised, and said, 'If we were not in a hurry, we would have waited for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), so convey our greetings to him,' and they went away.

So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) came back in anger, then said to them: 'The riders stopped by you and asked you about me, delivered the greeting to me, and you did not offer them lunch. It would be hard on a people in whom my dear friend Ja'far is, that they should pass by without having lunch with him.'

key_terms.جَعْفَرٌ: Ja'far (referring to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib or another companion known for hospitality)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on offering food to guests who pass by?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) expresses displeasure that his companions, while he was praying, failed to offer lunch (*al-ghada'*) to a passing caravan that had respectfully inquired about him and conveyed greetings. He invokes the memory of his close companion Ja'far (often identified as Ja'far al-Tayyar or a specific companion depending on the exegesis) to illustrate that true intimacy with the Prophet entails generous hospitality, ensuring guests are not dismissed hastily. This narrative underscores the Shia emphasis on *adab* (etiquette) and the social obligation of feeding guests as a direct reflection of one's spiritual connection to the Ahl al-Bayt.
